episodes.title: Fast and Right: What Lean Six Sigma Really Is

lines.t: Welcome to Lean Six Sigma Path, the podcast that takes you from beginner to running real improvement projects. I'm Nadia. I've spent about fifteen years fixing business processes in banks, retailers and hospitals.
And I'm Theo. I run an operations team, I've heard the words Lean and Six Sigma in a hundred meetings, and I'm here to finally understand what they mean.

Perfect. Let's start with a story. A bank I worked with took thirty-two days to approve a mortgage. Everyone was busy. Everyone was working hard. So Theo, how much of those thirty-two days do you think someone was actually working on the application?
I'd guess... a week? Maybe five days of real work?
Less than four hours.
Four hours out of thirty-two days? Where did the rest go?

Waiting. Waiting for documents, waiting in someone's inbox, waiting for a manager's signature, and redoing forms that came in incomplete. That's the heart of this whole course. Most of the cost, delay and frustration in a business lives inside everyday processes, not in people being lazy.
So what exactly counts as a process?

A process is any repeatable set of steps that turns inputs into outputs for a customer. Approving an invoice. Onboarding a new client. Resolving a support ticket. Hiring someone. If it happens more than once, and someone is waiting for the result, it's a process.
And Lean is about speeding those up?

Lean is about delivering more value to the customer with less waste, by making work flow smoothly. It came from the Toyota Production System, which Taiichi Ohno and his colleagues built from the nineteen forties onward. Toyota's system rests on two pillars. Just-in-Time, which means make only what's needed, when it's needed. And Jidoka, which means build quality in: stop and fix things the moment something goes wrong.
So Lean asks: where does the time go?
Exactly. And Six Sigma asks a different question: how often do we get it wrong, and why?
Where does Six Sigma come from?

Motorola, in nineteen eighty-six. An engineer named Bill Smith is usually credited. Then General Electric made it famous in the mid nineties under Jack Welch. Sigma is the Greek letter statisticians use for standard deviation, which measures how spread out results are. A process running at six sigma produces about three point four defects per million opportunities.
Three point four per million. That sounds impossible for an office.

And you don't always need it. Most office processes run somewhere around three sigma, which is about sixty-seven thousand defects per million. Going from three to four sigma is already roughly a tenfold improvement. You pick the level the customer and the business case justify.
So why combine the two? Why not just pick one?

Because they cover each other's blind spots. Lean is fast. In a few days you can strip out obvious waiting and duplicate work. But Lean doesn't always explain why results vary. Six Sigma is precise. It uses data to find root causes of defects and variation. But running statistics on a process full of obvious waste is a waste in itself.
So Lean first to clear the clutter, then Six Sigma for the stubborn problems.

That's the practical rule. One more idea before we go further. W. Edwards Deming, one of the fathers of quality, argued that most problems come from the system, not the people in it. So when an invoice gets paid late, we don't ask who messed up. We ask what about the process allowed it to happen.
That's going to be a hard sell in some of the meetings I attend.
It is, but it's also why people end up loving this work. When you stop blaming, people start telling you where the real problems are.
You mentioned belts. I always see Green Belt, Black Belt on LinkedIn. What do they mean?

They're skill levels, borrowed from martial arts. A White Belt knows the vocabulary. A Yellow Belt is a team member who understands the tools and contributes. A Green Belt leads smaller projects part time while doing their normal job. That's where this course takes you. A Black Belt leads complex projects full time, and a Master Black Belt coaches and trains the Black Belts.
And who's the boss of a project?

Two important roles. The Champion, or sponsor, is a senior leader who picks projects that matter and removes roadblocks. And the process owner runs the process day to day. That person keeps the improvement alive after the project team moves on.
Okay. Time for a quick check?

Yes. Every episode ends with three questions. I'll ask, you'll get a few seconds to answer in your head, then we'll give the answer. Ready? Question one. In one sentence, what does Lean focus on, and what does Six Sigma focus on?
Lean focuses on waste and flow, how fast work moves. Six Sigma focuses on variation and defects, how often we get it right.
Question two. A process at six sigma produces roughly how many defects per million opportunities?
About three point four.
Question three. Who keeps an improvement in place after the project closes?
The process owner.
Great. Three takeaways. One: most delay in business processes is waiting, not working. Two: Lean asks where the time goes; Six Sigma asks why results vary. Three: blame the process, not the person.
Next time, we learn to see waste. All eight kinds of it.
Head to module one in the course for the full lesson and quiz. See you next episode.

episodes.title: Seeing Waste: The Eight Wastes in Office Work

lines.t: Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. And today Nadia promised to ruin my inbox forever.

I did. Once you learn to see waste, you can't unsee it. But first, the five principles of Lean, from Womack and Jones' book Lean Thinking. Number one: value. Define value from the customer's point of view.
Meaning what they'd actually pay for.

Right. Two: the value stream. Map every step that delivers that value, end to end, across departments. Three: flow. Make those steps run without stopping, queuing or batching. Four: pull. Only start work when the next step or the customer asks for it. And five: perfection. Repeat the cycle. Each pass shows you more waste.
How do I decide whether a step adds value?
Three tests, and all three must be true. The customer cares about it. It actually changes the product or service. And it's done right the first time.
What about steps that are required, like a compliance check?

Good catch. Those are business-value-added. The customer doesn't value them, but the law or a risk policy requires them. Think of a know-your-customer check when opening a bank account. You keep those, but you make them as lean as possible. Everything else, the waiting, the rework, the chasing, is non-value-added. That's what we remove.
How much of a typical office process is real value?
Often less than ten percent of the elapsed time. Sometimes under one percent.
Okay, the eight wastes. Go.
There's an acronym: DOWNTIME. D is for defects. Errors that need fixing. A wrong invoice amount, a missing field, a shipment to the wrong address.
O?
Overproduction. Producing more, or earlier, than needed. The forty-page weekly report nobody reads. Printing copies just in case. It's often called the worst waste because it creates all the others.
W is waiting, I assume.

Waiting. An approval sitting in an inbox. A customer on hold. A team idle because a system is down. N is non-utilised talent. Your expert analyst spending half the week copying data between systems. Or staff who are never asked how to improve their own work.
That one stings. T?
Transportation. Moving the work unnecessarily. Emailing the same spreadsheet through five departments. Routing paper forms between buildings.
And how is that different from motion?
Motion is the person moving. Walking to the printer twenty times a day, or clicking between six different apps to find one customer record. Transportation is the work moving; motion is you moving.
Got it. I?

Inventory. Work piled up beyond what's needed. A backlog of eighteen hundred tickets. Four hundred unread emails. And finally E, extra-processing. Doing more than the customer needs. Three signatures to buy a fifty dollar item. Re-typing data that already exists in another system. Formatting a slide deck nobody will see.
So DOWNTIME. Defects, overproduction, waiting, non-utilised talent, transportation, inventory, motion, extra-processing.

Perfect. Now, Toyota has three related words. Muda is waste, those eight. Mura is unevenness, like month-end close where workload explodes for three days. And muri is overburden, pushing people beyond capacity.
And they connect?

They feed each other. Uneven demand creates overload at the peak, and overloaded people make mistakes, which creates rework. So one of the most powerful fixes in finance teams is simply levelling the work: doing reconciliations weekly instead of all at month-end.
How do I find waste in my own team without a big project?

Go to the gemba. It means the real place, where work happens. For an office, that might be a shared inbox, a queue in your ticketing system, or the screen a clerk uses. Follow one item, one order or one claim, from start to finish. Ask what are you waiting for, and what makes this step hard. And never use it to judge people.
Any example from real life?

A procurement team followed a single purchase request. It touched four systems, was printed twice, waited six days for a manager who approved ninety-nine percent of requests without changes, and then got re-typed into the finance system by a buyer. In one afternoon they found waiting, extra-processing, transportation, motion and defects.
Quiz time?
Quiz time. Question one. A team emails a spreadsheet through five departments for comments. Which waste is that mainly?
Transportation. The work is moving.
Question two. A mandatory anti-money-laundering check. Value-added, business-value-added or non-value-added?
Business-value-added. Required, but the customer doesn't pay for it.
Question three. Month-end creates a huge spike in workload. Which Japanese word describes that unevenness?
Mura.
Takeaways. One: value is defined by the customer. Two: DOWNTIME gives you eight lenses to spot waste. Three: go and see the real work before you redesign it.
Next episode: drawing the process, and the numbers that tell you how healthy it is.
Module two has the full lesson. See you there.

episodes.title: Mapping the Process and the Numbers That Matter

lines.t: Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Today is maps and maths. I'm told there's a law.
Little's Law. It's the single most useful equation in process improvement, and it fits on a sticky note. But let's start with maps. The first one is called a SIPOC.
Sounds like a sneeze.

It stands for Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers. It's a one-page, high-level view that sets the boundaries of your project. Take invoice processing. Suppliers are vendors, purchasing and the receiving dock. Inputs are the invoice, the purchase order and the goods receipt. The process is five to seven big steps: receive, scan, match, resolve exceptions, approve, pay. Outputs are a paid invoice and a ledger entry. Customers are the vendors, the finance controller and the auditors.
Why only five to seven steps?
Because it's a scoping tool, not the detailed map. A tip: fill it in starting from the process, then outputs, then customers, then inputs, then suppliers.
And the detailed map?

A swimlane map. Each role or department gets its own horizontal lane, and you draw the steps in order. Every time the flow crosses from one lane to another, that's a hand-off. And hand-offs are where work waits, information gets lost and mistakes creep in.
So more lane crossings, more trouble.
Usually. Map it as it really is, workarounds included, not as the procedure manual says. Walk the process with the people who do it.
Then what's a value stream map?

A value stream map adds data to each step. For each step you record process time, which is hands-on touch time, the wait time before the step, and something called percent complete and accurate: the share of work the next step can use without fixing or chasing it. At the bottom you draw a timeline that separates waiting from working.
Give me numbers.

Same invoice process. Receive and scan: wait one day, five minutes of work. Three-way match: wait two days, ten minutes. Resolve exceptions: wait three and a half days, twenty-five minutes. Manager approval: wait four days, three minutes of work. Schedule payment: wait one and a half days, seven minutes.
So about twelve days of waiting and fifty minutes of work.

Exactly. Which brings us to the metrics. Lead time is the total elapsed time the customer feels, here twelve days. Process time is the hands-on time, fifty minutes. And process cycle efficiency is value-added time divided by lead time.
Fifty minutes over twelve working days... that's under one percent.
About zero point nine percent. Very normal for office work, and a huge opportunity.
Okay, Little's Law.

Lead time equals work in progress divided by throughput. If a claims team has six hundred claims in progress and finishes fifty a day, the average claim takes six hundred divided by fifty: twelve days.
So to cut lead time I either finish more per day, or have less in progress.

And reducing work in progress is usually far cheaper. Stop starting, start finishing. If that team caps work in progress at three hundred while still finishing fifty a day, lead time halves to six days, without hiring anyone.
That's almost too simple.
It's simple, but people resist it, because starting things feels productive. Now one more metric: takt time. It's the pace of customer demand. Available time divided by customer demand.
Example?

An onboarding team has four hundred and fifty productive minutes a day and receives ninety new clients a day. Takt is four hundred fifty divided by ninety: five minutes. A new client arrives, on average, every five minutes. If onboarding one client takes twenty minutes of work, you need at least twenty divided by five, which is four people, just to keep pace.
And if you have three?

The backlog grows every single day. One last warning: don't trust averages alone. A step that averages two days might usually take two hours and occasionally three weeks when someone's on leave. Customers feel the spread. Record ranges or percentiles.
Quiz?
Question one. A team has three hundred open requests and completes twenty-five a day. What's the average lead time?
Three hundred divided by twenty-five. Twelve days.
Question two. Customer demand is two hundred and forty orders in a four hundred eighty minute shift. What's takt time?
Four hundred eighty divided by two hundred forty. Two minutes per order.
Question three. On a swimlane map, where do delays and errors usually cluster?
At the hand-offs, where work crosses lanes.
Takeaways. One: SIPOC scopes, swimlanes show hand-offs, value stream maps add the numbers. Two: most lead time is waiting. Three: Little's Law says cut work in progress to cut lead time.
Next episode: the Lean toolbox. Kanban, bottlenecks and error-proofing.
Module three has the calculators to practise. See you soon.

episodes.title: The Lean Toolbox: Flow, Bottlenecks and Error-Proofing

lines.t: Welcome back. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Last time we found the waste. Today we fix it?
Today we open the Lean toolbox. First tool: 5S. Sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain.
That's tidying the office, isn't it?

It looks like tidying, but the real purpose is to make problems visible and stop people wasting time searching. In a digital workplace, sort means archiving obsolete files and templates. Set in order means an agreed folder structure and naming rules. Shine means cleaning data and fixing broken links. Standardise makes it routine. Sustain makes it a habit, maybe a fifteen-minute monthly check.
Next?

Standard work. The current best way to do a task, written down and used by everyone. In offices that's checklists, templates, decision rules like approve automatically if under five hundred dollars and on contract. Without a standard, you can't tell whether a change is an improvement, because everyone was doing it differently anyway.
But doesn't that make work rigid?
Only if it never changes. The people doing the work own the standard and update it. If your standard work hasn't changed in two years, improvement has stopped.
Fair. What about kanban? Our IT team uses kanban boards.

Kanban is a pull system. In a push system, work starts the moment it arrives, and gets shoved onto the next step whether it can cope or not. Queues grow, priorities get lost. In a pull system, a step only starts new work when there's capacity. A kanban board shows columns for each stage, cards for each item, and a work-in-progress limit on each column.
And Little's Law says less work in progress means shorter lead time.

You were listening! A marketing team I worked with had forty-six campaigns in progress and delivered about five a week. Lead time: around nine weeks. They set a work-in-progress limit of twelve. Same throughput, so lead time dropped to under three weeks. Stakeholders got campaigns sooner, and fewer were abandoned halfway.
What about batches? We approve invoices once a week.

Batches create waiting for every item in them. Picture five forms going through three steps, one minute each. In a batch, step one handles all five, then passes them all on. The first form is finished after eleven minutes, the last after fifteen. In one-piece flow, each form moves on the moment it's done. The first form is finished after three minutes, the last after seven.
Same work, same people, way faster.

Batches exist because switching tasks has a setup cost. Shrink the setup and small batches become economical. That's SMED, single-minute exchange of die, from Shigeo Shingo. The office version: prepare templates, access and data before month-end, not during it.
Okay, bottlenecks.

A process can only go as fast as its slowest step, the constraint. Eliyahu Goldratt's Theory of Constraints gives five focusing steps. Identify the constraint. Look for the biggest queue. Exploit it: make sure it never sits idle and only does work only it can do. Subordinate everything else: don't flood it. Elevate it: add capacity, automate, cross-train. Then repeat, because the bottleneck will move.
So if claims assessment can only handle sixty a day and demand is eighty...

The queue in front of assessment grows by about twenty claims a day. Speeding up intake or payment changes nothing. First, take admin work away from assessors and make sure intake only sends complete files. Stagger lunch breaks so assessment never stops. Then cross-train approvers, who have spare capacity, to handle simple cases.
An hour saved anywhere else is an illusion.

Right. Next: poka-yoke, Japanese for mistake-proofing. Design the process so errors are impossible or instantly obvious. Drop-down lists instead of free text. Mandatory fields. A bank account number that's checked by a validation rule. A warning when you enter a duplicate invoice.
Better than training people to be careful.

Much better. Think of a ladder. Strongest: eliminate the step entirely. Then make the error impossible. Then detect it immediately. Then inspect afterwards. Weakest: train people and hope they remember.
And kaizen?

Kaizen means change for the better: small continuous improvement by everyone. A kaizen event is a focused three to five day workshop. Day one: walk the process and map it. Day two: find waste and design the future state. Days three and four: implement and test. Day five: report out to leaders and agree the follow-up list.
Quiz.
Question one. In Goldratt's five focusing steps, what comes right after identify the constraint?
Exploit it.
Question two. A form field that only accepts a valid ten-digit account number. Prevention or detection?
Prevention. You can't enter the error.
Question three. Why does reducing batch size cut lead time?
Because each item doesn't have to wait for the rest of the batch before moving on.
Takeaways. One: pull and work-in-progress limits create flow. Two: improve the bottleneck, not everything. Three: mistake-proof the process rather than relying on memory.
Next time we switch to Six Sigma and learn to count defects properly.
Module four in the course has the kanban and bottleneck diagrams. See you there.

episodes.title: Counting Defects: Sigma, Yield and the Hidden Factory

lines.t: Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo, and I'm slightly nervous because today has numbers.

Friendly numbers, I promise. Let's define some words. A unit is the thing being processed: an invoice, a call, an order. A defect is any failure to meet a customer requirement. A defective is a unit with one or more defects.
So an invoice with three errors is three defects but one defective.

Exactly. And an opportunity is a distinct chance for a defect that the customer cares about. Defects per million opportunities, or DPMO, equals defects divided by units times opportunities, times one million.
Example please.

An accounts payable team processes two thousand invoices. Each has five opportunities: vendor, amount, account code, due date and purchase order match. An audit finds one hundred eighty defects. Two thousand times five is ten thousand opportunities. One hundred eighty divided by ten thousand is zero point zero one eight. Times a million: eighteen thousand defects per million. That's about three point six sigma.
How does DPMO turn into a sigma level?

Through a standard table that assumes the normal curve and a one point five sigma long-term drift. Roughly: three sigma is sixty-seven thousand per million. Four sigma is about six thousand two hundred. Five sigma, two hundred thirty-three. Six sigma, three point four.
So each step up is a massive improvement.

Three to four is about ten times better. Five to six is about seventy times better. One caution: be honest about opportunities. If you count fifty opportunities per invoice, your sigma level looks fantastic, but the customer's experience hasn't changed.
Sneaky. What's yield?

First-pass yield is the share of units that get through a step right the first time, with no rework. Rolled throughput yield multiplies the first-pass yields of every step together. It's the chance a unit gets all the way through without anyone fixing anything.
Give me a feel for it.
Six steps. Each step is ninety-five percent right first time. Sounds good, right?
Sounds great.

Multiply zero point nine five by itself six times and you get about seventy-three and a half percent. More than a quarter of all work needs fixing somewhere. We call that the hidden factory: a whole shadow operation of corrections and re-dos that never shows up in the final numbers.
That's a bit terrifying.

It's also where the money is. Which brings us to cost of poor quality. Internal failure: rework, corrections and write-offs caught before the customer sees them. External failure: refunds, credit notes, complaints, penalties, lost customers. Appraisal: audits and inspections. And prevention: training and mistake-proofing, the good kind of spend. Industry estimates often put the total at fifteen to twenty-five percent of revenue for companies around three to four sigma.
So quantifying that is how I get a sponsor to care.

Exactly. Now, what does the customer actually want? Voice of the customer is what they say: complaints, surveys, calls, reviews. It's usually vague. I want fast refunds. Six Sigma turns that into a critical-to-quality requirement you can measure. Refund credited within three business days of approval, ninety-five percent of the time.
So a need, a driver, and a measurable target.

Right. And the Kano model helps you prioritise. Basic needs only cause anger when missing. Nobody's delighted their bill is correct, but they're furious when it's wrong. Performance needs give more satisfaction the better you do, like speed. And delighters surprise people, like proactive text updates. Over time, delighters become basic needs.
Like free shipping.

Perfect example. Finally, the roadmap: DMAIC. Define the problem. Measure how bad it is. Analyze to find root causes. Improve by fixing those causes. Control to hold the gain. Each phase ends with a tollgate review with the sponsor. If you're designing a brand new process instead, there's a sister roadmap called DMADV: Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify.
Quiz.
Question one. Five hundred orders, four opportunities each, sixty defects. What's DPMO?
Five hundred times four is two thousand. Sixty over two thousand is zero point zero three. Thirty thousand DPMO.
Question two. Four steps with first-pass yields of ninety-eight, ninety, ninety-five and ninety-nine percent. Roughly what's rolled throughput yield?
Multiply them... about eighty-three percent.
Question three. A credit note issued after a customer complains about a wrong invoice. Which cost category?
External failure.
Takeaways. One: count defects against honest opportunities. Two: rolled yield reveals the hidden factory. Three: turn vague customer needs into measurable requirements.
Next episode, we start DMAIC properly with Define.
Module five has a sigma calculator in the toolkit. See you next time.

episodes.title: Define: Choosing and Framing the Right Problem

lines.t: Welcome back. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. We're officially in DMAIC. Phase one, Define.

And Define is where most projects are won or lost. Let's start with picking the project. A good one connects to strategy, has a measurable problem, an unknown root cause, a scope you can finish in three to six months, and a sponsor who cares.
And a bad one?
A solution in disguise. Implement a new CRM. Or a scope like fix customer service. Or no data at all. If you already know the answer, just do it. You don't need DMAIC.
So the problem statement. How do I write a good one?

State what is wrong, where, when, how big, and the impact. No causes, no blame, no solution. Let me read you a weak one. Refunds are too slow because the finance team is understaffed, and we need a new system.
That has blame and a solution.

And no numbers. Here's a strong version. From January to June, customer refunds for online orders took an average of nine point four business days from request to credit, against a target of three days. Forty-one percent of refund-related contacts were repeat where's my refund calls, costing an estimated three hundred thousand dollars a year and lowering satisfaction scores among affected customers.
That's way more convincing. Nobody can argue with it.

And it doesn't make anyone defensive. Then the goal statement. It must be SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Reduce average refund lead time from nine point four to four business days by the thirty-first of March, with ninety percent of refunds completed within five days.
Why four and not three, which is the target?

A common rule for a first project is to aim to close about half the gap. You can always run another cycle. Now, the charter. It's the contract between the team and the sponsor. Business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team, timeline, risks.
And something called a guardrail metric?

Yes, and people forget it. A guardrail is what must not get worse. If you speed up refunds by removing checks, fraud might rise. So fraud rate becomes a guardrail. Same with cost per refund, or customer complaints.
Scope creep must be a huge problem.

It's the classic killer. Use an in-scope, out-of-scope list. In scope: online refunds, from request to money credited. Out of scope: in-store returns, supplier claims, replacing the finance system. When someone says, and while you're at it, could you also fix returns processing, it goes on a parking lot list or becomes another project.
How do I deal with all the people involved?

Map stakeholders by influence and interest. High influence and high interest: manage closely. That's your sponsor and process owner. High influence, low interest: keep satisfied, like the finance director or IT director. Low influence, high interest: keep informed. Often that's front-line staff, and they're your best source of ideas. Low and low: monitor.
And who decides what?

A RACI chart. Responsible does the work. Accountable owns the outcome. Consulted gives input. Informed is kept up to date. One rule: only one person is accountable for each task. If two people are accountable, nobody is.
What if my sponsor wants it done in four weeks and gives me a team for two hours a week?

Make the trade-off visible. Show what DMAIC needs. Then offer options: narrow the scope, run a focused kaizen week instead, or extend the timeline. And get the agreed team time written in the charter. A project that fails because it was impossible damages the whole program.
Quiz.
Question one. Which belongs in a good problem statement: the suspected cause, the proposed solution, or the size and impact of the problem?
The size and impact.
Question two. Why is implement a new ticketing tool a poor Six Sigma project?
Because the solution is already decided. There's nothing to analyze.
Question three. In a RACI chart, how many people should be accountable for a task?
Exactly one.
Takeaways. One: problem statements describe facts and impact, never blame or solutions. Two: add a guardrail so you don't break something else. Three: protect your scope.
Next: Measure, where we learn to trust our data.
Module six has practice charters to rewrite. See you then.

episodes.title: Measure: Trustworthy Data, Baselines and Capability

lines.t: Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Measure phase. I already have a dashboard. Am I done?

Maybe. But can you trust it? Let's find out. Start with the core idea of Six Sigma: Y equals f of X. Y is the outcome you care about, like refund lead time. The X's are the inputs and factors that drive it: channel, payment method, approval rules, staffing. You can't manage Y directly. You manage the X's.
So in Measure, I measure Y and start collecting the X's.
Exactly. Now, types of data. Continuous data is measured on a scale: time, cost, weight. Discrete data is counted. Counts, like errors per invoice. Or attributes, like pass or fail, yes or no.
Does it matter which?

A lot. Continuous data carries much more information per data point. Was the refund on time, yes or no, tells you less than how many days it took. And you can always turn days into on-time or late later. You can't go the other way.
Next is defining things, I'm guessing.

Operational definitions. Refund lead time sounds obvious until you ask: does it start when the customer clicks the button, when the request lands in the queue, or when the item is returned? Do weekends count? Write it down precisely, with the exact system fields, so two people measuring the same refund get the same number.
And then I collect data.

With a data collection plan. What you'll measure, how it's defined, where the data comes from, how much, who collects it, and how you'll display it. Collect the X's at the same time: region, product, team, channel, day of the week. That's called stratification, and it's often where the answers hide.
What's this MSA I keep reading about?

Measurement system analysis. Observed variation is real process variation plus measurement error. If the measurement is noisy, you'll chase problems that don't exist. For continuous data, a Gage R and R study checks repeatability, the same person getting the same result twice, and reproducibility, different people getting the same result. Under ten percent of total variation is good. Over thirty percent is unacceptable.
And for things like judging if a call was resolved?

Attribute agreement analysis. I once had three quality reviewers score the same thirty recorded calls. They agreed with each other only sixty-eight percent of the time on whether the call was resolved. We rewrote the definition with examples, retrained, and got to ninety-four percent before collecting any baseline data.
Otherwise the whole project would've been built on sand.

Exactly. Now describing data. The mean is the average. The median is the middle value, and it isn't pulled around by outliers. For lead times, which usually have a long tail of slow cases, report both. Standard deviation measures spread. For a normal bell curve, about sixty-eight percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, ninety-five within two, and ninety-nine point seven within three.
And the charts?

Histograms show shape. If you see two humps, you probably have two different processes mixed together, like two teams working differently. Run charts show data over time, so you see trends and shifts. Pareto charts sort categories from biggest to smallest. And box plots compare groups side by side.
Okay, capability. That's Cp and Cpk?

Yes. Capability compares the voice of the process, its natural spread, with the voice of the customer, the specification limits. Cp is the spec width divided by six standard deviations. It tells you whether the process could fit if it were centred. Cpk takes the closer limit into account: the distance from the mean to the nearest spec limit, divided by three standard deviations.
Example.

Calls must be handled in under ten minutes. Mean is seven, standard deviation is one point two. Cpk is ten minus seven, which is three, divided by three times one point two, which is three point six. So Cpk is about zero point eight three.
Is that good?

Not capable. Under one means a meaningful share of calls go over the limit. One to one point three three is marginal. One point three three or more is generally considered capable. And only calculate capability on a stable process. Check with a control chart first.
Quiz.
Question one. Time to approve a loan in hours. Continuous or discrete?
Continuous.
Question two. A histogram of lead times shows two distinct peaks. What's the likely explanation?
Two different groups or processes mixed together. Split the data.
Question three. Upper limit twenty, lower limit eight, mean sixteen, standard deviation one point five. What's Cpk?

Upper side: twenty minus sixteen is four, over four point five, about zero point eight nine. Lower side: eight over four point five, about one point seven eight. The smaller one wins. Zero point eight nine.
Takeaways. One: define every metric precisely. Two: check your measurement system before trusting the data. Three: capability compares the process with what the customer needs.
Next time, Analyze. Root causes, finally.
Module seven has the capability calculator. See you there.

episodes.title: Analyze: Finding and Proving Root Causes

lines.t: Welcome back. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Today we play detective.

We do. Analyze works like a funnel. Brainstorm many possible causes, then narrow them with data and logic to a few verified root causes. The most common mistake is fixing the cause everyone believes in, instead of the one the data supports.
Where do I start?

A fishbone diagram, also called an Ishikawa diagram. Write the problem at the head, then group possible causes along the bones. For services, use categories like people, process, systems, inputs, measurement and environment or policy. For our slow refunds: people, no backup approver. Process, refunds are approved in twice-weekly batches. Systems, the warehouse confirms returns by manual email. Inputs, customers give the wrong bank details. Measurement, nobody tracks ageing refunds. Policy, the bank file cut-off is at two p.m.
That's a lot of suspects.

It is. Next tool: the five whys. Why was the refund late? It waited four days for manager approval. Why? The manager approves in a batch on Tuesdays and Fridays. Why a batch? Every refund needs approval, about three hundred a week. Why every refund? A fraud incident three years ago led to a blanket rule. Why still blanket? Nobody checked it against current data. Ninety-six percent of refunds are small, and fraud there is negligible.
So the root cause is an outdated policy, not a slow manager.

Exactly. And check every why with evidence. Now Pareto analysis. Sort the delay reasons from biggest to smallest. Waiting for approval, forty-four percent. Warehouse confirmation, twenty-seven. Wrong payment details, fourteen. Those three account for eighty-five percent of delays. The vital few.
The eighty-twenty rule.

Roughly. Then for risks, FMEA: failure mode and effects analysis. For each step, list how it can fail, the effect, the cause and current controls. Score severity, occurrence and detection from one to ten. Multiply them to get the risk priority number.
And high detection score means bad?
Yes, and people get it backwards. A ten means you almost certainly won't catch it before the customer does. And always act on very high severity failures, nine or ten, whatever the total score.
Now the statistics part.

Let's start with correlation. A scatter plot shows two continuous variables together. The correlation coefficient r runs from minus one to plus one. And R squared tells you the share of variation in Y explained by X. An R squared of zero point six four means sixty-four percent is explained.
But correlation isn't causation.

Never. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Hot weather drives both. In business: tickets handled by senior agents take longer. Is it because seniors are slow, or because they get the hardest tickets? Always look for the lurking variable.
Hypothesis tests next. They always confused me.

Think of a courtroom. The null hypothesis is innocence: there's no difference. You need strong evidence to reject it. The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference this large if there really were no difference. If p is below your threshold, usually zero point zero five, you reject the null. People say, if p is low, the null must go.
And the errors?

Type one error: a false alarm. You reject the null when it was true. Type two: a missed signal. You fail to reject when there really was a difference. Bigger samples reduce type two errors. And remember, statistically significant isn't the same as important. With a hundred thousand records, a difference of six seconds can be significant and meaningless.
How do I pick the test?

Ask what kind of data your Y and X are. Continuous Y, two groups: two-sample t-test. Three or more groups: ANOVA. Continuous but heavily skewed: non-parametric tests that compare medians. Proportions, like error rates, between two groups: two-proportion test. Counts across categories, like complaint type by region: chi-square. And continuous Y and continuous X: correlation and regression.
Quiz.
Question one. A test comparing lead times for two teams gives a p-value of zero point zero two. Alpha is zero point zero five. What do you conclude?
Reject the null. The means are likely different. Then find out why, without blaming the team.
Question two. Which test compares average processing time across four regional offices?
One-way ANOVA.
Question three. FMEA: severity eight, occurrence five, detection six. What's the risk priority number?
Eight times five is forty, times six is two hundred forty.
Takeaways. One: brainstorm widely, then verify with data. Two: correlation is a clue, not proof. Three: match the test to the data type.
Next episode: Improve. We finally get to fix things.
Module eight has the fishbone and Pareto diagrams. See you next time.
Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Improve phase. I have about thirty ideas already.
Hold them for a moment. The first rule of Improve: every solution must link to a verified root cause. If it doesn't, it's a pet idea. Make a simple table. Root cause, solution, expected effect on Y.
For the refund case?

Root cause: blanket approval on all refunds. Solution: auto-approve refunds under a threshold when there's no fraud flag. Expected effect: removes about three and a half days of waiting for most refunds. Root cause: manual warehouse confirmation. Solution: scanning the returned item updates the system automatically. Root cause: wrong payment details. Solution: refund to the original payment method by default.
Where do ideas come from?

Brainstorming, but do silent writing first so quieter people contribute. Benchmarking against other teams or companies. A checklist called SCAMPER: substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to other use, eliminate, reverse. And Lean design principles: remove steps, combine hand-offs, move checks to where errors are created, run steps in parallel, create a fast lane for simple cases.
What about automation? Everyone wants robots now.

The rule is simplify, then standardise, then automate. Automate a messy process and you get a fast messy process. Before buying robotic process automation, ask: does this data entry step need to exist at all? Could the data be captured once, at the source?
How do I choose between ideas?

Start with an impact-effort matrix. High impact, low effort: quick wins, do them now. High impact, high effort: major projects, plan them. Low impact, low effort: fill-ins. Low impact, high effort: drop them.
And for the harder decisions?

A Pugh matrix. Put the options in columns and the criteria in rows, each with a weight. Compare every option to a baseline, usually the current process. Score each criterion better, same or worse. Add up the weighted scores.
Does the highest score win?

Often the best answer is a hybrid. In our refund case, auto-approval scored well on speed and cost but worse on fraud risk. Daily approval scored well on risk. So the team combined them: auto-approve small refunds with fraud flags, daily approval for larger ones. The hybrid fixed each option's weak spot.
Then we roll it out?

Not yet. First, draw the future-state map. Then pilot. Use the PDCA cycle: plan, do, check, act. Plan: what you'll change, where, for how long, your success criteria and guardrails. Do: run the pilot in one team or one region. Check: compare results to the baseline with data. Act: adopt, adapt or abandon.
What would the refund pilot look like?

One warehouse, card and PayPal refunds under four hundred dollars, six weeks, about fifteen hundred refunds. Success: median lead time three days or less, ninety percent within five days. Guardrail: fraud losses no higher than today. Stop criteria: fraud above an agreed limit, or payment file errors. Then compare before and after with a control chart and a statistical test.
And something called DOE?

Design of experiments. When several factors might interact, changing one at a time is slow and misses interactions. A designed experiment changes several factors together in a planned way. Three factors at two levels each is two to the power of three: eight runs. An A/B test on a website is the simplest example. At Green Belt level, know when it fits and get help from a Black Belt to plan it.
Last thing. Should I run a risk check on the new process?
Always. A quick FMEA on the future state catches new failure modes your changes create. Like auto-approval making it easier to commit fraud.
Quiz.
Question one. What must every proposed solution be linked to?
A verified root cause.
Question two. High impact, low effort ideas are called what?
Quick wins.
Question three. A two-level full factorial experiment with four factors needs how many runs?
Two to the power of four. Sixteen.
Takeaways. One: solutions target verified root causes. Two: simplify, standardise, then automate. Three: pilot with guardrails before rolling out.
Next time, Control. How to stop everything sliding back.
Module nine has the Pugh matrix example. See you there.
Welcome back. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Control phase. I've seen too many improvements quietly die.

So have I. People leave. Workarounds creep back. A system update reverses a setting. And the old KPI still rewards the old behaviour. Control is about making the new way the easy way, and spotting quickly when something changes.
Where do we start?

With two kinds of variation. Common cause is the natural noise of a stable process, lots of small causes. Special cause is an unusual event you can point to: a system outage, a new untrained hire, a supplier change.
Why does the difference matter?

Because the responses are opposite. Special causes: find and fix them. Common cause: you can only reduce it by changing the process itself. Deming warned about tampering: reacting to normal noise as if it were special. A manager who changes staffing every time output dips a little actually makes variation worse.
And control charts tell them apart.
Exactly. A control chart plots data over time with a centre line, the average, and control limits about three standard deviations either side, calculated from the process data itself.
Not from the customer's targets?
Never. Control limits are the voice of the process. Specification limits are the voice of the customer. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in the field.
Which chart do I use?

For continuous data, one measurement at a time, like daily median lead time: the individuals and moving range chart, I-MR. Small subgroups of two to nine: the X-bar and R chart. Bigger subgroups: X-bar and S. For attribute data, if you're counting defectives, pass or fail units, use a p chart when sample sizes vary, or np when they're constant. If you're counting defects, use a c chart with a constant area of opportunity, or a u chart when it varies.
That's a lot to remember.

The course has a decision chart. Now, the signals. One point beyond a control limit. A run of eight or so points on one side of the centre line, which signals a shift. Six points in a row steadily rising or falling, which signals a trend. Two out of three points beyond two standard deviations on the same side.
And after a successful project, I want to see...
A sustained shift in the good direction. Then recalculate limits from the new stable period.
Okay. What goes in the control plan?

It's the handover document. For each thing you monitor: what you're measuring, the target, the method, how often, who owns it, and the reaction plan. For example: refund lead time, median two days or less, I-MR chart on the daily median, checked daily by the process owner. Reaction: any rule violation is investigated within one working day and the cause is logged.
And the fraud guardrail?
Weekly fraud report, owned by the refunds lead. If fraud goes above half a percent, lower the auto-approval threshold and review with the risk team within forty-eight hours.
What else keeps gains alive?

Remember the ladder. Error-proofing beats procedures. Procedures beat training. Training beats reminders. Update the standard work, training and onboarding. Change the KPIs so they reward the new behaviour. Put the metrics on the team's board and talk about them in the daily huddle. Audit at thirty, sixty and ninety days.
And closing the project?
Confirm results with finance so savings are validated, not claimed. Document lessons learned. Celebrate the team. And share the solution with other sites that could copy it.
Quiz.
Question one. Control limits are calculated from what?
The process data itself. Not customer specs.
Question two. Daily proportion of late orders, when the number of orders varies each day. Which chart?
A p chart.
Question three. Nine consecutive points above the centre line. What does that suggest?
A shift. A special cause.

Takeaways. One: tell common cause from special cause, and don't tamper. Two: control limits come from the process, specs from the customer. Three: hand over a control plan with owners and reaction plans.
Next time, the people side. Leading change.
Module ten has the control chart chooser. See you there.

episodes.title: Leading Change: People, A3 and Strategy

lines.t: Welcome back to Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. Today's topic might matter more than all the statistics.

It often does. Many practitioners use a simple formula: E equals Q times A. The effectiveness of a change equals the quality of the solution times its acceptance. A brilliant solution with zero acceptance delivers zero.
So how do I get acceptance?

Start with each person. The ADKAR model from Prosci describes what an individual needs: Awareness of why change is needed. Desire to support it. Knowledge of how to change. Ability to actually do it. And Reinforcement to make it stick.
So if someone resists, I find out which step they're stuck on.

Exactly. If someone is stuck on desire, more training won't help. That's a knowledge fix for a desire problem. At the organisation level, Kotter's eight steps help: create urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a vision, communicate it, remove obstacles, generate short-term wins, consolidate gains, and anchor the change in the culture.
What about the classic fear? This will cost jobs.

Treat resistance as information. Ask what people fear losing: control, status, competence, their job. Then be honest. Get a clear answer from your sponsor on how freed capacity will be used. Clearing a backlog, handling growth without hiring, more time for complex cases. Say it clearly, and keep the promise. And involve the people who do the work. People support what they help create.
Okay. What's an A3?

Toyota's one-page problem-solving report, named after the A3 paper size. The left side is understanding: background, current condition, goal, root cause analysis. The right side is action: countermeasures, an implementation plan, and follow-up. It follows PDCA, and it's lighter than a full DMAIC deck.
Good for smaller problems.

And for coaching. A manager reads your A3 and asks questions on each box. Then there's hoshin kanri, or strategy deployment. Leadership sets a few breakthrough objectives. Each level translates them into its own goals and projects through catchball, a back-and-forth conversation about what's feasible.
Why does that matter for Lean Six Sigma?

Because the classic failure of improvement programs is a hundred small projects with certificates and claimed savings that don't add up to anything the CEO cares about. Strategy deployment links projects to what really matters, and finance validates the savings.
And in today's world, where does all this fit with automation and AI?

Process mining tools rebuild the real process from system event logs: case ID, activity, timestamp. It's a value stream map drawn from data, showing every variation and rework loop. Automation and AI amplify whatever process you apply them to, so simplify first. Business process management gives you governance: process owners and a process architecture. And agile teams already share Lean ideas: small batches, work-in-progress limits, retrospectives.
What's my path from here, practically?

Finish the course and the capstone. Aim for eighty percent or more on the final exam. Learn a statistics tool. Minitab, JMP, or free options like Python or R. Even Excel covers the basics. Then lead one real project at work, ideally with a mentor. Most credible Green Belt certifications require a completed project. Pick a certification body, like ASQ or IASSC, and read their body of knowledge to find gaps. And keep a portfolio of every project.
Quiz.
Question one. What does E equals Q times A mean?
Effectiveness of change equals quality of the solution times acceptance.
Question two. Name the five ADKAR elements in order.
Awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement.
Question three. Why is an A3 called an A3?
Because it fits on one sheet of A3 paper.
Takeaways. One: acceptance multiplies everything. Two: diagnose resistance with ADKAR. Three: link projects to strategy so the results matter.
Next episode is the finale. We run a full project together.
Module eleven covers all of this in more depth. See you for the capstone.

episodes.title: Capstone: A Full DMAIC Project, Start to Finish

lines.t: Welcome to the final episode of Lean Six Sigma Path. I'm Nadia.
I'm Theo. And today I'm the Green Belt. Nadia is my coach.

Let's set the scene. Northwind Living is an online furniture and homeware retailer with about one hundred eighty thousand orders a year. Refunds have become the top complaint. About twelve hundred refund requests a month. Average lead time from request to money credited: nine point four business days. Median eight, ninetieth percentile sixteen. The website promises five days.
So we're breaking our own promise.
Badly. Theo, you're in Define. What's your problem statement?

From January to June, Northwind refunds took an average of nine point four business days from request to credit, against a published promise of five days. That generated about twenty-one hundred status contacts and thirty-five chargebacks a month, costing around one hundred sixty-nine thousand dollars a year, and customers with refunds score us much lower than average.
How did you get that cost?

Twenty-one hundred contacts a month, seven minutes each, at ninety cents a minute. That's about thirteen thousand two hundred dollars a month, or roughly one hundred fifty-nine thousand a year. Plus thirty-five chargebacks a month at twenty-five dollars, about ten and a half thousand a year.
Nice. Goal?

Reduce median refund lead time from eight to three business days, with ninety percent completed within five days, by the end of March, without increasing fraud losses above today's level of zero point one five percent.
You remembered the guardrail. Now Measure. What does the data's shape tell you?

The mean is higher than the median, and the ninetieth percentile is sixteen days. So it's right-skewed, with a long tail of slow refunds. I'll report the median and percentiles, and use tests that work on skewed data.

Good. Now Analyze. Here's the Pareto of four hundred eighty-two refunds that took over five days. Manager approval wait, forty-four percent. Warehouse confirmation, twenty-seven. Wrong payment details, fourteen. Payment file errors, eight. Other, seven.
The top three cover eighty-five percent. So: blanket manager approval done in twice-weekly batches. Warehouse confirming returns by manual email. And bank details collected by free-text email.
Your sponsor says we just need more refund clerks. What do you say?

That the clerks aren't the constraint. Their validation step takes a few minutes. Most of the nine days is waiting for approval batches and warehouse emails. More clerks would add capacity where there's no queue. Lead time would barely move.
Exactly the right answer, delivered politely. What hypothesis would you test?
That refunds requested on Wednesday or Thursday wait longer, because they just miss Tuesday's batch and wait for Friday. I'd compare lead time by weekday.
Nice. Improve. Three solutions?

One: risk-based approval. Auto-approve refunds under four hundred dollars with no fraud flags, since nearly all fraud cases are above four hundred. Daily approval for bigger ones. Two: warehouse scan-to-confirm, so scanning the returned item updates the system and triggers the refund. Three: refund to the original payment method by default, and a validated form when bank transfer is needed.
And how do you protect against fraud?
Fraud rules flag repeat refunders and address mismatches. A weekly fraud report as the guardrail. And a random audit of two percent of auto-approved refunds.
Pilot?

One warehouse, card and PayPal refunds under four hundred dollars, six weeks. Success means median three days or less and ninety percent within five. Stop if fraud goes above an agreed limit or payment files start failing.
And finally, Control.

The process owner is the head of customer operations. A control chart on daily median lead time, checked daily, with a reaction plan. Weekly fraud rate against the threshold. Daily warehouse scan compliance. Standard work and training updated. Any change to the approval threshold needs sign-off from the process owner and the risk team. Audits at thirty, sixty and ninety days, and savings validated by finance.
Theo, that's a Green Belt answer.
I'll take it. Final quiz?
Final quiz. Question one. Why not just hire more clerks?
They're not the constraint. The delays are waiting for approval and confirmation.
Question two. What guardrail metric did we set?
Fraud losses as a percentage of refund value.
Question three. Lead time data with mean nine point four and median eight. What shape?
Right-skewed.
That's the series. You've gone from what is Lean to running a full DMAIC project. Now try the capstone in the course yourself and take the final exam.
And then find a real process at work, and fix it.
Thanks for listening to Lean Six Sigma Path. Go make something flow.
